title: Switches and MAC tables
summary: How a switch learns where every device is, and when it floods.

steps.title: A switch learns
body: A **switch** forwards Ethernet frames by **MAC address**. It keeps a **MAC address table**: which port each MAC was last seen on.
For every frame arriving on port P:
2. **Forward**: if the destination MAC is in the table, send it out that one port only.
3. **Flood**: if it's unknown, or the broadcast `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, send it out every port **except P**.
Entries age out (typically 300 s), so moved devices are relearned. A hub, by contrast, floods everything: every device sees every frame.
> **Practise for real:** **Labs → Live network labs** runs real Linux hosts, switches and routers you can poke at.

steps.prompt: PC A (port 1) pings PC B (port 3) on a switch with an empty table. Order what happens.
lines: A broadcasts an ARP request; switch learns A on port 1 and floods it
B replies to A's MAC; switch learns B on port 3
Switch forwards the reply only out port 1
A sends the ping to B's MAC; switch forwards it only out port 3
steps.explain: After one exchange both MACs are known and nothing is flooded any more.

steps.prompt: With A on port 1 and B on port 3 already learned, is each frame flooded or forwarded to one port?
items: Frame to a MAC never seen
ARP reply from B to A

steps.prompt: A security camera's traffic suddenly shows up on every port of the switch. Most likely?
options: The switch doesn't know the destination MAC (entry aged out or the table was flooded), so it floods unknown unicast
steps.explain: Unknown unicast flooding. An attacker can force it by filling the table with fake MACs (MAC flooding), which is why port security exists.

steps.title: MAC addresses
body: A MAC is 48 bits, written as 6 hex bytes: `3c:22:fb:12:34:56`.
- the first 3 bytes are the **OUI**, the vendor (`3c:22:fb` is one vendor's block);
- bit 0 of the first byte set means **multicast** (`01:00:5e:...` is IPv4 multicast); all ones is **broadcast**;
- bit 1 of the first byte set means **locally administered**: made up by software (VMs, containers, phones randomising MACs for privacy). Docker uses `02:42:...`.
Switches connected in a loop would flood broadcasts forever; **Spanning Tree Protocol** (STP) blocks redundant links to prevent that.

steps.prompt: Match each MAC to what it is.

steps.title: MAC helpers
prompt: Write `bool IsBroadcast(string mac)`, `bool IsMulticast(string mac)` (bit 0 of the first byte; broadcast counts), `bool IsLocal(string mac)` (bit 1 of the first byte)
and `string Oui(string mac)` (first three bytes, uppercase, `:`-separated). Accept `:` or `-` separators.
template: Dojo.Eq("vendor is not local", false, IsLocal("3C-22-FB-12-34-56"));
hints: Parse bytes with `Convert.ToByte(hex, 16)`; split on both `:` and `-`.

steps.title: A learning switch
prompt: Write a class `Switch` constructed with the number of ports (numbered 1..n):
- `List<int> Receive(int port, string src, string dst)` learns `src` on `port` and returns the ports the frame goes out of, ascending:
the known port of `dst` (or nothing if that's the port it came in on), or every other port for broadcast/unknown destinations.
solution: private readonly Dictionary<string, int> table = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
public List<int> Receive(int port, string src, string dst)
return outPort == port ? new List<int>() : new List<int> { outPort };
public int? PortOf(string mac) => table.TryGetValue(mac, out int p) ? p : null;
template: Dojo.Eq("unknown destination floods", new List<int> { 2, 3, 4 }, dojoS.Receive(1, dojoA, dojoB));
Dojo.Eq("reply goes to port 1 only", new List<int> { 1 }, dojoS.Receive(3, dojoB, dojoA));
Dojo.Eq("now B is known", new List<int> { 3 }, dojoS.Receive(1, dojoA, dojoB.ToUpperInvariant()));
Dojo.Eq("broadcast floods", new List<int> { 1, 2, 4 }, dojoS.Receive(3, dojoB, "ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff"));
Dojo.Eq("same port: filtered", new List<int>(), dojoS.Receive(1, dojoC, dojoA));
Dojo.Eq("moved device relearned", new List<int> { 4 }, dojoS.Receive(2, dojoC, dojoA));
